1.title: Security Services and Resources
1.text: Welcome to Module five: Security Services and Resources. This module finishes the second domain of the exam, Security and Compliance, with task statement two point four. You will learn which A W S service blocks attacks, which one detects threats, which one scans for weaknesses, and where to find more security information. Expect questions that describe a need and ask you to name the service.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Match A W S W A F, A W S Shield and A W S Firewall Manager to the threat each one stops. Tell Amazon GuardDuty, Amazon Inspector, Amazon Macie, Amazon Detective and A W S Security Hub apart. Choose among A W S K M S, A W S CloudHSM and A W S Certificate Manager, and say what A W S Resource Access Manager does. Use A W S Trusted Advisor to spot security gaps. And know where to find third-party security products and A W S security information.

1.title: Case Check-In: Tidewater Prepares for the Sale
1.text: Tidewater's holiday sale is near, and the shop sits behind a load balancer that is open to the internet. Last year, bots and traffic floods slowed the site, and someone tried S Q L injection in the search box. The team worries about stolen credentials, unpatched servers, and customer addresses stored in S three. The shop now uses several A W S accounts, and only two people look after security. Your job is to pick the tools to block, detect, scan and review, and to know where to learn more.

1.title: The Security Toolbox at a Glance
1.text: Start with the whole toolbox, grouped by job. To block attacks before they reach the application, there are three: A W S W A F, A W S Shield and A W S Firewall Manager. To detect and investigate threats, there is Amazon GuardDuty and Amazon Detective. To find weaknesses, there is Amazon Inspector, Amazon Macie and A W S Trusted Advisor. To collect every finding in one place, there is A W S Security Hub. And to protect keys, certificates and sharing, there is K M S, CloudHSM, Certificate Manager and Resource Access Manager. Exam tip: each service has one main job, so read the verb in the question: block, detect, scan, discover or investigate.

1.title: AWS WAF: Filtering Web Requests
1.text: A W S W A F is a web application firewall. It inspects the H T T P and H T T P S requests that are sent to your application. You attach it to Amazon CloudFront, an Application Load Balancer, Amazon A P I Gateway rest A P Is, A W S AppSync and other supported resources. Its rules sit in a web A C L, short for access control list. The newer console calls that a protection pack, but exam material still says web A C L. A rule can allow, block or count a request, or ask the visitor to solve a captcha. You can match on I P addresses, headers and query strings, and a rate-based rule limits requests that arrive too fast. Managed rule groups block common attacks, such as S Q L injection and cross-site scripting. Exam tip: web exploits and bad bots at the application layer point to A W S W A F.

1.title: AWS Shield: Standard and Advanced
1.text: A D D O S attack floods a target from many systems, so real users cannot get in. A W S Shield protects against it in two levels. Shield Standard is automatic, with no extra charge, and defends against the most common network and transport layer attacks. Every customer gets it, and the benefit is strongest for Route fifty-three, CloudFront and Global Accelerator. Shield Advanced is a paid subscription for the resources you add, such as CloudFront, Route fifty-three hosted zones, Global Accelerator, Elastic I P addresses and load balancers. It adds expanded protection, automatic layer seven mitigation with W A F, the Shield Response Team, cost protection as service credits, and health-based detection. As of the fourth of November, twenty twenty-six, the Response Team needs a paid support plan, and plan names are changing, which Module fourteen covers. Exam tip: free and automatic means Standard; response team and cost protection mean Advanced.

1.title: AWS Firewall Manager: One Policy, Many Accounts
1.text: A W S Firewall Manager sets protections up once and applies them across the accounts and resources in A W S Organizations. It manages W A F rules, Shield Advanced, security groups and network A C Ls, A W S Network Firewall, and Route fifty-three Resolver D N S Firewall. You scope a policy to all resources of a type, or to resources with specific tags. The key benefit is that new accounts and new resources are protected automatically. On cost, you pay for the underlying services, such as W A F and A W S Config. Picture Tidewater with thirty accounts: one policy, applied everywhere, including accounts that do not exist yet. Exam tip: one place to manage firewall rules for many accounts means Firewall Manager.

1.title: Amazon GuardDuty: Threat Detection
1.text: Amazon GuardDuty is threat detection. It watches your account for suspicious activity, continuously. As soon as you turn it on, it analyzes CloudTrail management events, V P C flow logs and D N S logs. It compares what it sees with threat intelligence, such as known malicious I P addresses and domains, and uses machine learning. It finds things like compromised credentials, cryptomining and malware. Optional protection plans add more sources, such as S three, E K S, R D S logins, Lambda, malware scanning and runtime monitoring. Findings go to Security Hub, Detective and EventBridge, and new accounts get a thirty-day free trial. Exam tip: suspicious activity and compromised credentials point to GuardDuty.

1.title: Amazon Inspector: Finding Weaknesses
1.text: Amazon Inspector is vulnerability management. It looks for software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure. It scans Amazon E C two instances, container images in Amazon E C R, and A W S Lambda functions. Scanning is automatic and continuous. It rescans when you install a package, apply a patch, or when a new C V E is published. Each finding names the resource and suggests a fix, with a risk score adjusted to your environment. Findings flow to EventBridge and Security Hub. Here is a way to remember the difference from GuardDuty: GuardDuty asks, what is happening? Inspector asks, what could be exploited? Exam tip: known vulnerabilities on instances, images or functions point to Inspector.

1.title: Amazon Macie: Sensitive Data in S3
1.text: Amazon Macie finds sensitive data in Amazon S three, using machine learning and pattern matching. It detects personally identifiable information, which people shorten to P I I, plus financial information and credentials, and you can add your own custom data identifiers. It also keeps an inventory of your S three buckets and flags risks, such as a bucket that becomes publicly accessible. Automated discovery samples your buckets, while discovery jobs go deeper, once or on a schedule. Findings go to EventBridge and Security Hub, and new accounts get a thirty-day free trial. Exam tip: sensitive data, such as P I I, stored in S three points to Macie.

1.title: Amazon Detective: Finding the Root Cause
1.text: Amazon Detective helps you investigate a security finding and find its root cause. It collects CloudTrail logs, V P C flow logs and GuardDuty findings automatically. From them it builds a behavior graph, with visual summaries over time, and it keeps up to a year of history. That lets you answer questions such as, is this an unusual A P I call for this role? You can jump from a GuardDuty finding straight into Detective. Remember the pair: GuardDuty detects, Detective investigates. Exam tip: to detect, think GuardDuty; to investigate the root cause, think Detective.

1.title: AWS Security Hub: One View of Findings
1.text: A W S Security Hub gives you one view of your security state across accounts, A W S services and partner products. Look at the figure. GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie and partner products send their findings in. Security Hub also checks your setup against standards: the A W S Foundational Security Best Practices, C I S, P C I D S S, and N I S T. Automation rules and EventBridge can act on the findings. Most of its checks need A W S Config recording turned on. As of the fourth of November, twenty twenty-six, the documentation names the service A W S Security Hub C S P M, short for Cloud Security Posture Management, while the exam may simply say Security Hub. Exam tip: one place to see findings and standards checks from many services means Security Hub.

2.title: Keys and Certificates: KMS, CloudHSM and ACM
2.text: Three services handle keys and certificates, and the exam asks you to tell them apart. A W S K M S creates and controls the keys that encrypt and sign your data. Its keys sit in hardware security modules validated to F I P S one forty dash three, Level three, and key policies control who can use them. Choose it for a managed key service that works with A W S services. A W S CloudHSM gives you dedicated, single-tenant hardware security modules in your V P C. You control the keys, algorithms and users, so choose it when rules demand full control, and accept more responsibility. A W S Certificate Manager creates, stores and renews public and private S S L and T L S certificates for integrated services, so choose it for H T T P S on a load balancer or CloudFront. It adds no charge for certificates; you pay for the resources that use them. Exam tip: managed keys, K M S; your own dedicated hardware, CloudHSM; website certificates, Certificate Manager.

2.title: AWS Resource Access Manager: Share, Don't Copy
2.text: A W S Resource Access Manager, called ram, lets you share your resources with other A W S accounts, with an organization or an organizational unit, and for some resource types with I A M roles and users. You create a resource once, then share it, instead of building a copy in every account. A shared resource looks native in the other account. For example, a shared V P C subnet appears in the V P C console. The owner keeps ownership. A managed permission on the resource share sets what others may do, and their I A M policies and service control policies still apply. There is no additional charge for ram itself; you pay for the shared resource. Exam tip: share a resource with other accounts without duplicating it, and the answer is Resource Access Manager.

2.title: AWS Trusted Advisor: Security Checks
2.text: A W S Trusted Advisor inspects your account and recommends ways to save money, improve performance and availability, and close security gaps. Its checks fall into six categories: cost optimization, performance, security, fault tolerance, service limits, and operational excellence. Every account gets the service limits checks and a set of core security checks: S three bucket permissions, security groups with unrestricted ports, M F A on the root account, and public E B S and R D S snapshots. The full set of checks, and the A P I, need a paid support plan. As of the fourth of November, twenty twenty-six, the full set comes with Business Support plus, Enterprise Support or Unified Operations, while older material says Business or Enterprise Support. Exam tip: a quick review for security gaps points to Trusted Advisor, and the full set needs a paid plan.

2.title: AWS Marketplace: Third-Party Security Products
2.text: A W S Marketplace is a curated digital catalog where you find, test, buy and deploy third-party software. Its security listings come from independent software vendors, in areas such as application security, endpoint security, identity and access control, S I E M, W A F and edge security, and managed security services. Use it for a product your team already knows, or one that A W S does not offer as a service. Managed rules for A W S W A F can also come from Marketplace sellers. Remember that you still configure and operate what you deploy. Exam tip: a third-party security product, bought and deployed on A W S, means A W S Marketplace.

2.title: Where to Find Security Information
2.text: The exam guide also asks where security information is available. The A W S Security Blog publishes how-to guides, announcements and compliance news. The A W S Knowledge Center gives answers to common A W S questions, and it is hosted with A W S re:Post, where the community asks and answers questions. The guide also names the A W S Security Center. The A W S cloud security pages gather security services, learning, compliance, whitepapers and reference architecture, and there are pages to report vulnerabilities and suspicious emails. As of the fourth of November, twenty twenty-six, no page is titled exactly A W S Security Center; the cloud security pages play that role. Exam tip: learn from the Security Blog and Knowledge Center, and get A W S's compliance reports from A W S Artifact.

2.title: What the Exam Asks: Security Services
2.text: Here is how the exam frames these services. A web attack or a flood: W A F filters requests, and Shield absorbs D D o S attacks. Many accounts, one policy: Firewall Manager. Detect or scan: GuardDuty detects threats, and Inspector finds vulnerabilities. Discover or investigate: Macie finds P I I in S three, and Detective finds the root cause. See everything together: Security Hub. Keys, hardware or certificates: K M S, CloudHSM and Certificate Manager. And review or buy: Trusted Advisor reviews, and Marketplace sells third-party products. Exam tip: name the verb first, then the service.

2.title: Design Check: Tidewater's Security Plan
2.text: Now a design check. Cover the right column and answer each row yourself. S Q L injection and bad bots at the load balancer: W A F, with managed rule groups and a rate-based rule. Traffic floods during the sale: Shield Standard, which is automatic, and Shield Advanced for the most critical sites. The same web rules in every account, including new ones: Firewall Manager. Stolen credentials or cryptomining: GuardDuty, then Detective to find the root cause. Unpatched servers and container images: Inspector. Customer addresses stored in S three: Macie. One place for every finding: Security Hub. And open ports and public buckets, found quickly: Trusted Advisor. Pause the video if you want more time.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. To block: W A F filters web requests, Shield defends against D D o S, and Firewall Manager applies protections across accounts. To detect and investigate: GuardDuty finds threats, and Detective finds the root cause. To find weaknesses: Inspector scans for vulnerabilities, Macie finds sensitive data in S three, and Trusted Advisor checks for gaps. To collect: Security Hub brings findings and standards checks together. To protect: K M S manages keys, CloudHSM gives dedicated hardware, Certificate Manager manages certificates, and Resource Access Manager shares resources. And to learn and buy: Marketplace for third-party products, and the Security Blog, Knowledge Center and cloud security pages for information.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Tidewater's shop sits behind an Application Load Balancer, and attackers are sending S Q L injection strings in search requests. Which service can block these requests before they reach the application? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D, A W S W A F. It inspects H T T P and H T T P S requests and blocks patterns such as S Q L injection through rules and managed rule groups. Shield Standard defends against network and transport layer floods, Inspector finds vulnerabilities, and GuardDuty detects threats, but none of them filters web requests.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Which service continuously analyzes A W S CloudTrail events, V P C flow logs and D N S logs, using threat intelligence and machine learning, to detect suspicious activity such as cryptomining or compromised credentials? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A, Amazon GuardDuty. It is the threat detection service that watches those data sources and reports findings. Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities, Macie discovers sensitive data in S three, and Trusted Advisor recommends improvements from its checks.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. Select two. Which two benefits come with an A W S Shield Advanced subscription but not with A W S Shield Standard? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and D. Shield Advanced adds access to the Shield Response Team, which also needs a paid support plan, and cost protection in the form of service credits. Automatic, no-charge protection against common network and transport layer attacks is what Shield Standard already provides, and container image scanning is Amazon Inspector.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Tidewater now runs thirty accounts in A W S Organizations. The security team wants the same A W S W A F rules applied in every account, including accounts created later, from one place. Which service should it use? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C, A W S Firewall Manager. It applies W A F rules and other protections across accounts in an organization, and covers new accounts and resources automatically. Security Hub collects findings, GuardDuty detects threats, and Shield Standard is automatic but has no rules to manage.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. A new administrator wants a quick review of the account for security gaps, such as a publicly accessible Amazon S three bucket, security group ports left open, and a root user without M F A. Which A W S tool gives these recommendations? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B, A W S Trusted Advisor. It inspects the account and recommends fixes, and its core security checks include bucket permissions, unrestricted security group ports and M F A on the root account. Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities and network exposure, Artifact provides compliance reports, and Marketplace sells third-party software.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Tidewater wants a third-party endpoint protection product that A W S does not offer as a service. Where can it find, buy and deploy such security software on A W S? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A, A W S Marketplace. It is the catalog for finding, testing, buying and deploying third-party software, including security products. The Security Blog and Knowledge Center are places to learn, and Artifact provides A W S's own compliance reports and agreements.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all six answers. Question one: D. Question two: A. Question three: B and D. Question four: C. Question five: B. Question six: A. That completes Module five, and with it the Security and Compliance domain. Next, Module six begins the technology domain, with how you deploy and operate in the cloud, and the A W S global infrastructure.
